stubs.angle: What does a program print when an Account method changes the private _balance field of another Account instance passed as a parameter?
stubs.answerHinge: C# accessibility is checked per type, not per object, so code inside Account may read and write private members of any Account instance, and the snippet compiles and prints the moved balances.

stubs.angle: What happens when an int[] stored in an IList<int> variable is passed to code that calls Add on it?
stubs.answerHinge: Arrays implement IList<T> but are fixed size, so Add throws NotSupportedException at run time, a BCL case where the subtype does not honour the full interface contract and callers must check IsReadOnly.

stubs.angle: A PriceTiers class validates in its constructor that the limits array is sorted, yet after the caller changes its own array the object reports itself unsorted; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: The constructor assigns the caller's array reference to a readonly field without a defensive copy, so the caller can mutate the object's state after validation; copying the array (ToArray or Clone) restores the invariant.

stubs.angle: Which of the listed members can a C# 14 interface not declare: a static field, a private method with a body, a default implementation, a static abstract method or an instance field?
stubs.answerHinge: Since C# 8 and C# 11 interfaces may contain default implementations, private and static members and static abstract members, but they still cannot hold instance state, so an instance field is the only illegal member and an abstract class remains the choice for shared state.

stubs.angle: What happens when class D implements IB and IC, and both of them provide an explicit default implementation of IA.M, while D itself declares no M?
stubs.answerHinge: With two equally specific default implementations of IA.M the compiler cannot pick one and reports CS8705 (no most specific implementation), so the class must implement the member itself.

stubs.angle: In what order does a program print messages from a derived field initializer, the base constructor body and the derived constructor body?
stubs.answerHinge: In C# the instance field initializers of the derived class run before the base constructor is invoked, so the order is derived initializer, base constructor, derived constructor body.

stubs.angle: Which changes made by an override break substitutability for code written against the base class contract?
stubs.answerHinge: A subtype breaks LSP when it strengthens preconditions, weakens postconditions or throws exceptions the base contract does not allow, while accepting wider input or returning more specific results keeps it substitutable.

stubs.angle: Why do the .NET design guidelines suggest sealing classes that were not designed for extension, and what does sealing or unsealing later mean for consumers?
stubs.answerHinge: A class open to inheritance exposes its internal call sequence as a contract that derived classes rely on, so types not designed for extension are sealed; unsealing later is a compatible change while sealing an existing public class breaks derived types.

stubs.angle: Which way of declaring Customer.Email guarantees that no Customer object can exist with an empty email: a required init property, a [Required] attribute, a property with a default empty string, or a constructor that validates and assigns a get-only property?
stubs.answerHinge: The C# 11 required modifier only forces the caller to assign the member and attributes are checked only by a validator that someone must run, so only validation in the constructor (or in the accessor) enforces the invariant on every instance.

stubs.angle: An IRepository with 25 methods is implemented by six classes, half of which throw NotImplementedException, and every change to it forces edits and rebuilds in unrelated modules; what do you do?
stubs.answerHinge: NotImplementedException in implementations signals both an ISP violation and broken substitutability, so the fix is to split the interface into role interfaces by what each client actually calls and migrate clients incrementally.

stubs.angle: A team standard requires an interface for every class, so the codebase has hundreds of single-implementation header interfaces and navigation is painful; how do you revise the policy?
stubs.answerHinge: Interfaces pay off at real seams (I/O boundaries needed for tests, several implementations, module or package boundaries, role interfaces owned by the client), so the policy should require them there and drop mechanical one-to-one header interfaces.

stubs.angle: Your team cites YAGNI to reject any up-front design; when is it still right to invest in flexibility before the need is confirmed?
stubs.answerHinge: YAGNI targets presumptive features, not the cost of change, so up-front design is justified where reversal is expensive, such as published APIs and contracts, persisted data formats and public library surface, while cheaply refactorable internal code waits for the real need.

stubs.angle: For a NuGet library used by many teams, which default visibility for new types best limits future breaking changes?
stubs.answerHinge: Making an internal type public later is a compatible change while reducing the visibility of a public type breaks consumers, so new types should be internal until a consumer needs them.

stubs.angle: Which .NET code analysis rules would you enable to make the team keep encapsulation in public types: CA1051, CA2227, CA1002, CA1822 or CA2007?
stubs.answerHinge: CA1051 (no visible instance fields), CA2227 (collection properties should be read-only) and CA1002 (do not expose generic lists) guard encapsulation, while CA1822 is about marking members static and CA2007 about ConfigureAwait.

stubs.angle: A platform team ships BaseController, BaseService and BaseEntity classes that thirty services must inherit from; why does this become a liability over years and what would you offer instead?
stubs.answerHinge: Inheritance at platform scale turns the fragile base class problem into an organisation-wide coupling where any change to base class internals can break every service, so cross-cutting behaviour should be offered through composition (middleware, decorators, small interfaces and helpers) with few deliberate extension points.

stubs.angle: A Company.Common NuGet package with utilities and domain models is used by thirty services and every release forces coordinated upgrades; how do you apply DRY across service boundaries?
stubs.answerHinge: Code shared between independently deployed services couples their release cadence, so share only stable, domain-agnostic, semantically versioned infrastructure and let each service own its domain types even at the cost of duplication.
